books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

source: original; stimulus is an original account drawn from the grounding books

stimulus.source_note: Account drawn from the grounding books (5 Steps Ch. 27; Princeton Ch. 12; Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.10). The June 21, 1964 murder date, the three names, and the Atlantic City compromise are in the books and the standard accounts (Library of Congress and the National Archives on Freedom Summer and the MFDP).
stimulus.text: In the summer of 1964 about a thousand volunteers, most of them white college students from the North, came to Mississippi for Freedom Summer. They joined local Black organizers to register Black voters and to teach in Freedom Schools. On June 21, 1964, three of the workers, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner, were murdered near Philadelphia, Mississippi, after being arrested and released by local police. Their bodies were found six weeks later. The murders drew national attention to the violence facing Black Mississippians who tried to vote. That August the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party (MFDP), led by sharecropper Fannie Lou Hamer, went to the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City and asked to be seated as Mississippi's true delegation, since Black Mississippians had been kept from voting in the regular party. The convention offered the MFDP two at-large seats instead, and the MFDP refused them.

stem: The murders of Chaney, Goodman, and Schwerner best show which of the following about Mississippi in 1964?

options.text: Voter registration work there was welcomed by local police
options.misconception: The three were arrested by local police and then murdered after their release.

options.text: The federal government had already registered every Black voter in the state
options.misconception: The passage describes volunteers still trying to register Black voters, not a finished job.

options.text: Northern students refused to work with local Black organizers
options.misconception: The passage says the volunteers joined local Black organizers.

options.text: Trying to register Black voters could be met with deadly violence

rationales.A: Local police arrested the three men shortly before they were murdered.
rationales.B: Volunteers were still registering voters, so the work was not finished.
rationales.C: The volunteers joined local Black organizers; they did not refuse to work with them.
rationales.D: The passage says the three workers were murdered after being arrested and released by local police.
rationales.general:
1. Three voter-registration workers are arrested by local police in Mississippi.
2. After their release they are murdered near Philadelphia, Mississippi.
3. Their bodies are found six weeks later, after a long search.
4. The murders show that registration work in Mississippi could be deadly.
Remember: The cost of a protest is measured in what happened to the protesters who carried it out.
